Clear denominators and compare coefficients, or substitute convenient x-values, to find all four constants.
Recombine the result to verify the original rational function.
walkthrough:
Expand the denominator of $f(x)$ to check polynomial degrees:
$$(3 + x)(2 + x^2) = 6 + 3x^2 + 2x + x^3 = x^3 + 3x^2 + 2x + 6$$
$$\text{Since numerator and denominator both have degree 3, perform polynomial division:}$$

Set up the partial fraction decomposition for the proper remainder:
$$\dfrac{-3x^2 - 17}{(3 + x)(2 + x^2)} = \dfrac{B}{3 + x} + \dfrac{Cx + D}{2 + x^2}$$
$$-3x^2 - 17 = B(2 + x^2) + (Cx + D)(3 + x)$$

Equate coefficients of $x^2$ to find $C$:
$$-3 = B + C \implies -3 = -4 + C \implies C = 1$$

Equate constant terms ($x = 0$) to find $D$:
$$-17 = 2B + 3D \implies -17 = 2(-4) + 3D$$
$$-17 = -8 + 3D \implies 3D = -9 \implies D = -3$$

State the full partial fraction decomposition:
$$f(x) = 1 - \dfrac{4}{3 + x} + \dfrac{x - 3}{2 + x^2}$$

hints: Retain terms only through x², but multiply the second series by its linear numerator before truncating.
Add the constant from part (a), collect like powers, and simplify the coefficients.
walkthrough:
Rewrite the first partial fraction into standard binomial form:
$$-\dfrac{4}{3 + x} = -\dfrac{4}{3\left(1 + \dfrac{x}{3}\right)} = -\dfrac{4}{3}\left(1 + \dfrac{x}{3}\right)^{-1}$$

Expand $\left(1 + \dfrac{x}{3}\right)^{-1}$ up to $x^2$ using $(1 + u)^{-1} = 1 - u + u^2 - \dots$:
$$-\dfrac{4}{3}\left[1 - \dfrac{x}{3} + \left(\dfrac{x}{3}\right)^2\right] = -\dfrac{4}{3}\left[1 - \dfrac{1}{3}x + \dfrac{1}{9}x^2\right] = -\dfrac{4}{3} + \dfrac{4}{9}x - \dfrac{4}{27}x^2$$

Rewrite and expand the second partial fraction up to $x^2$:
$$\dfrac{x - 3}{2 + x^2} = (x - 3)\left(2\left(1 + \dfrac{x^2}{2}\right)\right)^{-1} = \dfrac{x - 3}{2}\left(1 + \dfrac{x^2}{2}\right)^{-1}$$
$$\left(1 + \dfrac{x^2}{2}\right)^{-1} = 1 - \dfrac{x^2}{2} + \dots$$
$$\left(\dfrac{1}{2}x - \dfrac{3}{2}\right)\left(1 - \dfrac{x^2}{2}\right) = -\dfrac{3}{2}(1) + \dfrac{1}{2}x(1) + \left(-\dfrac{3}{2}\right)\left(-\dfrac{x^2}{2}\right) = -\dfrac{3}{2} + \dfrac{1}{2}x + \dfrac{3}{4}x^2$$

Combine the constant term 1 with both expansions:
$$\text{Constant term: } 1 - \dfrac{4}{3} - \dfrac{3}{2} = \dfrac{6 - 8 - 9}{6} = -\dfrac{11}{6}$$
$$\text{Term in } x: \dfrac{4}{9} + \dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{8 + 9}{18} = \dfrac{17}{18}x$$
$$\text{Term in } x^2: -\dfrac{4}{27} + \dfrac{3}{4} = \dfrac{-16 + 81}{108} = \dfrac{65}{108}x^2$$

State the combined expansion up to the term in $x^2$:
$$f(x) = -\dfrac{11}{6} + \dfrac{17}{18}x + \dfrac{65}{108}x^2$$
